title: Workforce behind AI spans 160M workers, many in the Global South
content:
Many widely used artificial intelligence products depend on people to perform repetitive work to train and maintain the systems, even though the technology is often presented as if it runs on its own.
A significant share of those workers are paid low wages and live in the Global South. Focus on the AI boom is putting more attention on questions of pay, labor protections, and who ultimately benefits from growth in the industry.
Here's what to know
In an interview with Democracy Now! in late August, sociologist Antonio Casilli highlighted the largely unseen workforce behind commercial AI, including people handling data annotation and content moderation.
Casilli — author of Waiting for Robots: The Hired Hands of Automation and co-writer of the documentary In the Belly of AI — underscored that AI products often framed as self-sustaining still rely on workers to keep them operating.
In the interview, he said that workers "are purposely hidden by the companies that produce AI because they are the secret ingredient of AI itself."
According to Casilli, more than 160 million people worldwide are doing this data work. At that scale, AI looks less like a replacement for human labor than a restructuring of it, with difficult and poorly paid tasks often kept out of public view.
The interview arrived amid a wider debate about employment after Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates argued in a recent essay that AI could profoundly reshape jobs. In the essay, Gates wrote that "AI will either be the greatest equalizer ever invented, or the worst source of injustice."
More background
Public discussion often centers on AI as a future threat to jobs, but the technology is already changing working conditions for millions of people, many of whom live in low- and middle-income countries. Not only that, but many workers involved in training data and content moderation operate in fragmented gig-style arrangements that can be unstable, underpaid, and a risk to well-being.
Meanwhile, consumers and businesses are using chatbots, image generators, search tools, and recommendation systems without seeing the exploitative labor chain behind them. They may also be voting on AI-related policies, such as those regarding data center development, without understanding the human costs of the technology, even as AI company owners stand to reap huge financial rewards.
What's being done?
Some data workers are starting to organize and demand recognition for the role they play. Labor that stays hidden is easier to underpay, while greater transparency can increase pressure for better standards.
Among the demands emerging from that organizing are calls for fairer wages, employment protections, and equitable treatment.
Where can I learn more?
The human labor behind AI is one piece of a bigger story about the industry's rapid expansion. As companies pour money into growth, fights over jobs, security, and resources are intensifying:
• Public outcry against AI is rising over jobs, security, and resource use.
• Big Tech's $725 billion AI boom is pushing expansion faster than power grids can handle.
• Utilities are signing unprecedented deals with data centers as AI demand reshapes energy costs.
These developments put AI labor issues in a broader context, alongside strain on infrastructure, the environment, and public trust. Taken all together, they help explain why disputes over fair pay, protections, and accountability may be getting harder to ignore.

report.summary: AI's hidden human labor force spans 160M workers, mostly low-paid Global South data annotators, exposing inequities behind automation.
report.background: The rapid commercial growth of large language models, image generators, and recommendation engines depends on laborers who label data, review outputs, and moderate content. These tasks are frequently outsourced through opaque supply chains to low-income countries. Sociologist Antonio Casilli argues this hidden workforce is the 'secret ingredient' of AI, kept out of sight to sustain the illusion of fully autonomous systems. This pattern follows earlier digital outsourcing but has reached an unprecedented scale of an estimated 160 million workers. Public narratives about AI replacing human jobs obscure how automation is reorganizing work rather than eliminating it—often concentrating precarious, poorly paid tasks among vulnerable populations. Meanwhile, tech companies capture enormous value, invest in data centers and infrastructure, and shape policy outcomes, while consumers rarely see the human cost embedded in the products they use.
key_points: AI products are not self-running: Companies hide workers doing data annotation, labeling, and content moderation to preserve the fiction of autonomous systems. Casilli calls these employees the 'secret ingredient' of AI, and their invisibility makes it easier to underpay them and avoid accountability.

More than 160 million people worldwide perform this labor, most in the Global South. They often work in unstable gig-style arrangements with low pay and few employment protections. That geographic concentration means AI growth is restructuring labor globally, pushing the hardest parts of the value chain onto lower-income countries.

Popular debates focus on AI replacing jobs in the future, but current workers are already experiencing worsening conditions. Consumers, businesses, and policymakers use AI and vote on data-center policies without seeing exploitative supply chains, even as tech owners reap massive financial rewards and strain energy grids, raising wider public concerns.

Data workers are beginning to organize collectively for recognition, fairer wages, employment protections, and equitable treatment. Greater transparency—along with public fights over jobs, energy, and security—may force companies and regulators to treat labor standards as a core AI-governance issue, not an afterthought.
report.impact: Understanding AI’s human supply chain reshapes what 'automation' means. It is not just a future job threat but a present-day restructuring of work, with profits flowing to major AI firms while costs fall on low-wage workers in the Global South. For developers and companies relying on data annotation, ignoring labor conditions creates reputational, regulatory, and ethical vulnerability; humane wage standards, transparency, and worker consultation become crucial. For consumers and citizens, realizing that chatbots and image tools depend on hidden human effort weakens marketing claims of autonomous intelligence. It also sharpens policy debates around data centers, energy use, and tax incentives, since these decisions affect a vast workforce and may deepen global inequality. AI’s promised equalizing potential will only materialize if these workers gain visibility, protections, and a share of the value they help create.
report.tools: To follow these issues, watch the Fairwork project, which rates gig platforms on pay, conditions, and transparency. For crowd workers themselves, Turkopticon provides reviews of requesters, and the worker-led site We Are Dynamo offers organizing space. Researchers can also consult Antonio Casilli’s public materials and the documentary 'In the Belly of the AI' for deeper case studies.
